questions.stem: A patient presents with a puncture wound visibly contaminated with soil. Under current CDC tetanus wound guidance, how should this injury be classified for tetanus exposure risk?

options.text: Dirty or major wound
Clean and minor wound
No tetanus-risk wound
Classify only if clinical infection develops

questions.explanation: CDC categorizes penetrating or puncture wounds and wounds contaminated with soil as dirty or major wounds for tetanus-risk assessment.

questions.stem: An immunocompetent adult completed the primary tetanus vaccine series and received the last tetanus-containing vaccine 3 years ago. The patient now has a crush injury. What does current CDC wound guidance recommend regarding tetanus vaccination?

options.text: No tetanus vaccination is needed for this wound
Give a tetanus-containing booster now
Restart the primary tetanus series
Give TIG instead of considering vaccination

questions.explanation: When the primary series is complete and the most recent tetanus vaccination was less than 5 years ago, CDC does not recommend another tetanus vaccine regardless of wound type.

questions.stem: A patient with a complete tetanus primary series has a clean, minor laceration. The last tetanus-containing vaccine was 11 years ago. Which vaccination action is indicated under current CDC wound guidance?

options.text: Administer a tetanus-containing vaccine booster
No tetanus vaccination is indicated
Administer TIG without a vaccine
Give prophylactic antibiotics instead of vaccination

questions.explanation: For a clean and minor wound in someone with a complete primary series, CDC recommends a tetanus-containing vaccine when 10 or more years have elapsed since the last dose.

options.text: Administer a tetanus-containing vaccine booster
No tetanus vaccination is needed
Restart the entire primary series
Use TIG as a substitute for vaccination

questions.explanation: For dirty or major wounds in people with a complete primary series, CDC recommends a tetanus-containing vaccine when 5 or more years have elapsed since the last dose.

questions.stem: A patient with an unknown tetanus vaccination history presents with a dirty puncture wound. Which passive prophylaxis is indicated under current CDC wound guidance?

options.text: Tetanus immune globulin is indicated
Tetanus immune globulin is never indicated
Routine intravenous immunoglobulin is the preferred prophylaxis
Antibiotic prophylaxis replaces passive immunization

questions.explanation: CDC recommends tetanus immune globulin for dirty or major wounds when tetanus vaccination history is unknown, absent, or the primary series is incomplete.

questions.stem: A patient with sore throat also has cough, rhinorrhea, and hoarseness. According to current CDC group A streptococcal pharyngitis guidance, what is the appropriate testing approach?

options.text: Do not test for group A streptococcus when the viral features are clear
Perform a throat culture in every case
Perform a rapid antigen test in every case
Order streptococcal antibody serology for acute diagnosis

questions.explanation: CDC states that patients with clear viral symptoms can be diagnosed clinically with viral pharyngitis and do not need testing for group A streptococcus.

questions.stem: A school-age child has acute pharyngitis without cough, rhinorrhea, hoarseness, oral ulcers, or conjunctivitis. Which diagnostic approach is supported by current CDC guidance?

options.text: Use a rapid antigen detection test or throat culture to confirm group A streptococcal pharyngitis
Diagnose group A streptococcal pharyngitis by clinical examination alone
Use antistreptolysin O titre as the primary acute diagnostic test
No microbiologic testing is useful

questions.explanation: When clear viral symptoms are absent, clinical examination alone cannot reliably distinguish viral from group A streptococcal pharyngitis; CDC supports RADT or throat culture for confirmation.

questions.explanation: CDC advises that people with group A streptococcal pharyngitis remain home until afebrile and at least 12–24 hours after appropriate antibiotic therapy has begun.

questions.explanation: CDC includes people with pre-existing conditions that may be exacerbated by pertussis, including moderate-to-severe medically treated asthma, among those at high risk of severe infection.

Give repeated antibiotic courses to every contact indefinitely
Stop all surveillance and follow-up
Require weekly cultures from every exposed person

questions.explanation: When continued pertussis transmission is evident, CDC does not recommend multiple rounds of antibiotics and instead advises monitoring exposed people for symptoms for 21 days.

questions.explanation: CDC considers a vaccinated clinician with documented anti-HBs of at least 10 mIU/mL protected; no HBV postexposure prophylaxis is needed regardless of source HBsAg status.

Give HBIG only and do not vaccinate
